findings.F1: The panic premium is short-lived. Over all 1975 cases, the excess return over the coin's normal drift is +0.35 % over 6 bars (24 h, t 2.98). It is +0.02 % over 18 bars (3 days, t 0.12), then turns negative: -1.59 % over 42 bars (t -5.75) and -2.17 % over 84 bars (t -4.88). The 14-day horizon the book bets on sits where the effect has already reversed.
findings.F2: The book holds far past the premium. It made 3400 trades lasting 34.8 days on average, with a minimum holding of 84 bars. Its daily mean return of 0.047 % therefore mostly carries the coin's later fall, giving a deepest fall of -64.6 % on the chained book and a Calmar of 0.059.
findings.F3: The premium is large and lasting only in the most extreme panics of coins whose 60-day return was negative. In that group's top tercile of panic depth (196 cases), the excess is +1.84 % over 1 day (t 4.14, strength 0.36), +2.07 % over 2 days (t 3.75), +1.74 % over 7 days (t 2.35) and +2.13 % over 14 days (t 1.54). The bottom tercile of the same group shows -1.59 % over 3 days (t -3.02) and -2.91 % over 7 days (t -3.41).
findings.F4: Over all cases, panic depth barely grades the 14-day outcome (correlation of raw depth with the 84-bar excess 0.010). Over 1 day it does grade: the excess rises from +0.16 % in the bottom tercile (t 0.91) to +0.44 to +0.46 % in the upper two (strength 0.036 against 0.083 to 0.088).
findings.F5: Panics coming after a weak 7 days give the largest 1-day premium but the worst 14 days. In the bottom tercile of the 7-day return, the excess is +0.77 % over 1 day (t 2.74) and -3.10 % over 14 days (t -4.07). The top tercile gives +0.04 % over 1 day and -3.01 % over 14 days.
findings.F6: The book's losses come in falling markets. On days in the lowest quartile of the 20-day coin return, the book loses -0.75 % a day while the coins lose -1.12 %. In the top quartile it earns +0.50 % against the coins' +1.33 %. This leaves its Sharpe 0.27 below holding's.
findings.F7: On a 1-day horizon the move is large enough to cover the trade cost of 0.22 %. In the deepest-panic tercile of 60-day-negative coins, the total 1-day move is +2.01 %, 9 times the cost. Over all 60-day-negative cases it is +1.00 %.

ideas.idea: In coins whose 30-day return before the panic was negative, a 24-hour stretch with a range several times its 30-day average and a hard fall is followed by higher than usual returns over the next 1 day, rather than 14 days, and the more extreme the panic, the higher the return.
ideas.consequence: The liquidity premium is paid within a day of the forced selling, so a long taken on the panic earns it only when held for about a day, not for weeks of the coin's later drift.
ideas.name: one-day panic rebound

ideas.idea: In coins whose 60-day return before the panic was negative, a 24-hour stretch with a range several times its 30-day average and a hard fall is followed by higher than usual returns over the next 7 days, and the more extreme the panic, the higher the return, the premium lasting longer the deeper the panic.
ideas.consequence: Only the deepest panics after a 60-day decline justify holding the rebound for a week; shallower drops in such coins keep falling and are a reason to refuse the trade.
ideas.name: deep panic after decline

ideas.idea: In coins whose 30-day return before the panic was negative, a 24-hour stretch with a range several times its 30-day average and a hard fall is followed by higher than usual returns over the next 1 day, and the weaker the coin's 7-day return before the stretch, the higher that return.
ideas.consequence: A panic that ends a week-long slide offers the largest one-day rebound, which a trader should take and then leave, since the slide resumes over the following two weeks.
ideas.name: capitulation one-day rebound
